subject: Professional Knowledge
question: Write-ahead logging requires which order?
option_a: The changed data page reaches disk before any log record of that change
option_b: A checkpoint deletes the log before any data write
option_c: The log record of a change reaches stable storage before the changed data page does
option_d: Undo is never recorded, because recovery reads only the data pages
explanation: The diary of a change must reach the safe before the changed ledger page does. Otherwise a crash can leave a page that recovery cannot explain or undo. Remember: the log is written before the data page.
hint: If the crash happens between the two writes, the log must already explain the change.
hint_2: Writing the data page first can leave a change the log cannot undo, and a checkpoint does not delete the log.
hint_3: The log goes first. That is the write-ahead rule.

question: A sparse index contains an entry for which of the following?
option_a: Every search-key value in the data file
option_b: Only nulls
option_c: Only some blocks or groups of records, not every search-key value
option_d: Every non-key column of every row
explanation: A sparse index is like a chapter list that names some pages, not every line. One entry can cover a block or a group of records, whereas a dense index has an entry for every search key. Remember: sparse means some groups, and dense means every key.
hint: Dense means one index entry per search key. Sparse means fewer than that.
hint_2: An entry for every search key is the dense case, and nulls alone are not the definition.
hint_3: One entry can cover a block, so the index is shorter than the data.

exam_title: IBPS SO IT Mains — High-Influence PK Mock (50Q, 100 marks, 40 min)
subject: Professional Knowledge
question: A decomposition is lossless when the natural join of the parts does which of the following?
option_a: Always adds spurious tuples that were not in the original relation
option_b: Drops the candidate key in every case and cannot be joined
option_d: Requires a Cartesian product with no join attribute and still loses tuples
explanation: Splitting a table is lossless when joining the pieces brings back exactly the original rows, with nothing extra. Extra rows on that join mean the split lost information, even though it looks reversible. Remember: lossless means the join gives the original rows back, and nothing more.
hint: Extra rows are the sign of a bad split.
hint_2: Dropping the key, or joining with no shared column, is not the test.
hint_3: The natural join must restore the starting table exactly.

subject: Professional Knowledge
question: Which command is a DCL command?
option_a: UPDATE
option_b: CREATE
option_d: DROP

hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. CREATE and DROP are DDL. UPDATE is DML.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: GRANT is DCL.

subject: Professional Knowledge
question: A phantom read is which event?
option_a: A checkpoint that flushes dirty pages
option_b: A read of an uncommitted update that is later rolled back
option_c: Two writes of the same row with no intervening read
option_d: A second query in the same transaction sees a new row that another transaction inserted and committed
explanation: A phantom is a new committed row that appears when the same range query is run again inside one transaction, like a new account slipping into a list you already counted. A dirty read is a look at data that was never posted. Remember: a new row in a repeated range is a phantom.
hint: The same query, run twice, sees a different set of rows, and the new row was committed.
hint_2: An uncommitted value that disappears is a dirty read, and a checkpoint is recovery work.
hint_3: A new row appears in a range the transaction already queried.

question: A relation is in BCNF when which condition holds for every non-trivial functional dependency X determines A?
option_a: A is a non-prime attribute
option_b: A is transitively dependent on X
option_c: X is a single non-key attribute
option_d: X is a superkey
explanation: Boyce-Codd form looks at the left side of every real dependency, not only at non-key columns. The columns that decide the others must themselves be able to find each row uniquely. Remember: in this form, every column set that decides another column must be a key.
hint: Do not look only at whether the right side is a key column.
hint_2: A chain through a middle column is a failure here, not the rule itself.
hint_3: Ask whether the deciding columns can uniquely find the row.

exam_title: IBPS SO IT Mains — High-Influence PK Mock (50Q, 100 marks, 40 min)
subject: Professional Knowledge
question: TCP slow start grows the congestion window, until a threshold or a loss, in which way?
option_a: It adds one segment per round trip and never increases faster than that
option_b: It is set by a DNS response
option_c: It stays fixed at one segment for the life of the connection
option_d: It roughly doubles each round trip, because each acknowledgement increases the window by one segment
explanation: Picture a parcel between two programs, which may or may not ask for a receipt: In slow start, each acknowledgement increases the congestion window by one segment, so the window roughly doubles every round trip. After the threshold, congestion avoidance grows it more slowly. Remember: slow start doubles per round trip, despite the name.
hint: Picture a parcel between two programs, which may or may not ask for a receipt. The name slow start is historical. The growth itself is exponential in the round-trip count.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. Adding one segment per round trip is congestion avoidance, after the threshold. The window does not stay at one, and DNS does not set it.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: slow start doubles per round trip, despite the name.

question: Count-to-infinity is a problem of which routing style?
option_a: Link-state flooding, where every router has a full map
option_b: CSMA/CD
option_d: Distance-vector routing
explanation: Picture signboards between branches, some counting hops and some keeping a full map: In distance-vector routing, a router advertises distances and may accept a neighbour's route to a destination that actually goes through itself, so the metric climbs toward infinity after a failure. Link state avoids that by flooding the topology. Remember: count-to-infinity belongs to distance-vector routing.
hint: Picture signboards between branches, some counting hops and some keeping a full map. A router tells its neighbours a distance, and a failed route's distance climbs one hop at a time.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. Link state shares the map, so it does not count toward infinity in this way. Circuit switching and CSMA/CD are not routing-table exchanges.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: count-to-infinity belongs to distance-vector routing.

hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. 32 bits is IPv4. 48 bits is a common MAC-address length. 256 is not the address length.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: IPv6 is 128 bits.

subject: Professional Knowledge
question: A CRC on a frame is used mainly to do which of the following?
option_a: Correct any burst error by itself in the usual link check
option_b: Assign a MAC address
option_c: Choose a route between autonomous systems
option_d: Detect errors in the frame
explanation: Picture the receiver recomputing a check on a frame and comparing it with the check that arrived: A cyclic redundancy check detects errors by comparing a computed remainder with the received remainder. Correction, if any, is a separate mechanism such as retransmission. Remember: CRC detects, and a Hamming code is the usual correction example.
hint: Picture the receiver recomputing a check on a frame and comparing it with the check that arrived. The receiver recomputes a check and compares it with the received check.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. A usual CRC detects; it does not by itself tell the sender how to repair an arbitrary burst. Routing and MAC assignment are different jobs.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: CRC detects, and a Hamming code is the usual correction example.

hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. 0 is the previous block. 128 is the next block. 70 is a host address inside the block, not the network address.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: for a /26, clear the last 6 bits of the host address.

question: If the Round Robin time quantum is made extremely small, which effect dominates?
option_a: The scheduler behaves like First Come First Served
option_b: Context-switch overhead becomes a large fraction of CPU time
option_d: Belady's anomaly disappears from the pager
explanation: Picture a teller who serves each customer for a fixed short turn, then moves to the next: A tiny quantum causes a context switch after almost every brief run, so switch overhead dominates. hint: Picture a teller who serves each customer for a fixed short turn, then moves to the next. A very large quantum pushes Round Robin toward one familiar non-preemptive scheduler. A very small quantum does the opposite harm.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. First Come First Served behaviour appears when the quantum is huge, not tiny. Quantum size does not remove deadlock or Belady's anomaly.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: too small a quantum wastes the CPU on switching.

question: A zombie process is which of the following?
option_a: A process that has finished, but whose parent has not yet collected its exit status
option_b: A process running on two CPUs at the same moment by definition
option_c: A thread that holds no locks
option_d: A dirty page in the page cache
explanation: Picture the identity card the operating system keeps for each running job: A zombie has exited, but its parent has not collected the exit status, so the process-table entry remains. It is not a running process and not a dirty page. Remember: exited and not yet reaped means a zombie.
hint: Picture the identity card the operating system keeps for each running job. The process has exited. A small record remains until the parent calls wait.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. Two CPUs, an unlocked thread, and a dirty page are not the definition of a zombie.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: exited and not yet reaped means a zombie.

exam_title: IBPS SO IT Mains — High-Influence PK Mock (50Q, 100 marks, 40 min)
subject: Professional Knowledge
question: In deadlock avoidance, a state is safe when which of the following is true?
option_a: There is an order of process completions that can satisfy every remaining need from currently available resources, releasing each process's allocation as it finishes
option_b: Every process already holds at least one resource, which is required for safety
option_d: No process has declared a maximum claim
explanation: A state is safe when there is an order in which every process can get what it still needs, finish, and hand its resources to the others. The Banker's algorithm refuses a request that would leave no such order. Remember: safe means there is a way for every process to finish.
hint: Look for an order in which every process can finish.
hint_2: Already holding a resource is not what makes a state safe, and a deadlock is already stuck.
hint_3: A safe state has a completion sequence that never gets stuck.

question: Compaction is a remedy for which problem?
option_a: External fragmentation in variable-size memory allocation
option_b: A dirty read in a database
option_d: A weak password hash
explanation: Picture a small desk, with files brought from the cupboard only when a clerk needs them: Compaction moves allocated variable-size blocks so that scattered free holes become one usable region. It addresses external fragmentation, not a concurrency anomaly. Remember: holes between blocks, slid together, means compaction.
hint: Picture a small desk, with files brought from the cupboard only when a clerk needs them. Free memory exists, but it is broken into holes too small for the next request.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. A dirty read, a lost segment, and a weak hash are not fixed by sliding allocated blocks together.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: holes between blocks, slid together, means compaction.

question: A multilevel feedback queue changes a process's priority mainly according to which behaviour?
option_a: The length of the process name

option_d: The number of open SQL cursors only
explanation: The queue watches how the process actually uses the CPU, not a label fixed at the start. A process that burns its whole time slice sinks, and a process that blocks quickly, as interactive work often does, can stay higher. Remember: CPU-hungry work sinks, and interactive work can stay higher.
hint: The process name, the screen colour, and the number of SQL cursors are not the signal.
hint_2: The priority is feedback from observed behaviour.
hint_3: A process that uses its whole slice sinks.

question: The load factor of a hash table is which ratio?
option_a: The number of stored keys divided by the number of slots
option_b: The number of slots divided by the key size in bits
option_c: The chain length multiplied by the table's base address
option_d: The height of an AVL tree used as a secondary index in every hash table
explanation: The load factor is how full the pigeonholes are: stored keys divided by the number of slots. When that ratio climbs, chains and probe sequences get long, so the table is resized. Remember: load factor equals keys divided by slots.
hint: It measures how full the table is.
hint_2: Key size, a base address, and a tree height are not the load factor.
hint_3: Keys divided by slots is the ratio.

exam_title: IBPS SO IT Mains — High-Influence PK Mock (50Q, 100 marks, 40 min)

question: In a binary search tree, deleting a node that has two children is usually done by replacing it with which node?
option_a: Either child, with no further change to the tree
option_b: Its in-order successor or its in-order predecessor
option_c: The root of the whole tree, in every deletion
option_d: A newly inserted null node that becomes the parent of both children
explanation: A node with two children is replaced by the next key in sorted order, or the previous one, because that neighbour has at most one child and the search order stays intact. Copying either child in place can put a larger key on the left. Remember: two children means replace with the in-order neighbour.
hint: The replacement must keep every left descendant smaller and every right descendant larger.
hint_2: Either child can break the search order, and the root is not the general replacement.
hint_3: The next key in sorted order, or the previous one, can take the node's place.

question: In the usual case, C passes an argument by which method?

option_d: By a database trigger
explanation: Picture a C function receiving a photocopy of each argument, not the original paper: C passes arguments by value, so the function receives a copy and assigning to the parameter does not change the caller's variable. hint: Picture a C function receiving a photocopy of each argument, not the original paper. The callee can change its parameter without changing the caller's variable, unless an address was passed.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. C does not pass every int by reference. Pass by name is not the C rule. A trigger is not a calling convention.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: C is pass by value, and a pointer is how the callee reaches the original.

question: Basic two-phase locking divides a transaction into which sequence?
option_a: A growing phase, then a shrinking phase
option_b: A shrinking phase, then a growing phase
option_d: A phase that releases every lock before the first lock is acquired
explanation: Basic two-phase locking has a growing phase, when the transaction only takes locks, and then a shrinking phase, when it only gives locks back. Reversing that order is not two-phase locking. Remember: take locks first, and only then start giving them back.
hint: The transaction must not take a new lock after it has started releasing locks.
hint_2: Releasing first and acquiring later is the reverse of the rule.
hint_3: Growing, then shrinking.

question: A schedule is serial when which of the following is true?
option_a: Operations of different transactions are interleaved
option_b: The transactions run one after another, with no interleaving
option_c: Every read is a dirty read
option_d: The precedence graph is required to contain a cycle
explanation: Picture lining the same bank updates up, one customer after another: A serial schedule completes one transaction before the next begins, so their operations do not interleave. Interleaving is what a concurrent schedule adds. Remember: no interleaving means serial.
hint: Picture lining the same bank updates up, one customer after another. One transaction finishes before the next one starts.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. Interleaving is a concurrent schedule. Dirty reads and a cycle are failures, not the definition of serial.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: no interleaving means serial.

question: In SQL, COUNT(salary) differs from COUNT(*) because COUNT(salary) does which of the following?
option_a: Counts every row, including rows where salary is null
option_b: Counts only rows that fail the WHERE clause
option_c: Ignores rows in which salary is null
option_d: Counts distinct table names
explanation: COUNT of a column skips empty salaries, while COUNT star counts rows whether the salary is empty or not. A null salary therefore changes one count and not the other. Remember: COUNT of a column skips nulls, and COUNT star does not.
hint: Counting empty salaries as well is what counting rows does.
hint_2: Rows that fail WHERE are already gone before the count.
hint_3: The column form skips nulls.

hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: a view is a stored query, not a second base table.

question: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads?
option_a: Serializable
option_b: Read Uncommitted

hint: Read Uncommitted allows a dirty read.
hint_2: Read Committed still allows the same row to change on a second read.
hint_3: You want the strictest isolation level.

exam_title: IBPS SO IT Mains — High-Influence PK Mock (50Q, 100 marks, 40 min)

question: A B-tree index differs from a B+ tree index because a B-tree may store which of the following in an internal node?
option_a: Only a child pointer, with no key at all
option_b: A key together with a data pointer, not only a separator
option_d: A TCP sequence number
explanation: A B-tree may keep the actual record pointer beside a key inside the tree, so a search can stop before a leaf. A B+ tree keeps those record pointers only at the leaves and uses the inside nodes as signposts. Remember: a record pointer inside the tree can mean a B-tree, not a B+ tree.
hint: An inside node with no key cannot guide a search.
hint_2: The log and a TCP number are not index contents.
hint_3: The B-tree may store the data pointer before the leaf.

hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. A primary key identifies rows in its own table. Not-null on every column is stricter than this rule and is not the reference. ORDER BY only sorts.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: a reference to a parent key is a foreign key.

hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: undo uses the before-image, and redo uses the after-image.

option_a: The network layer
